subproblems.title: Weight of a closed ball as the integral of the multiplicity
subproblems.statement: Let n, ℓ ∈ ℕ and U ⊆ ℝ^{n+ℓ}. Let V = v(M, θ) be a rectifiable n-varifold in U (RectifiableVarifold n ℓ U) with carrier M and multiplicity θ. Let x ∈ ℝ^{n+ℓ} and r ∈ ℝ be such that the closed ball B_r(x) ⊆ U. Then μ_V(B_r(x)) = ENNReal.ofReal(∫_{M ∩ B_r(x)} θ dHⁿ), where Hⁿ = μHE[n].
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (U : Set (Amb n ℓ)) (V : RectifiableVarifold n ℓ U) (x : Amb n ℓ) (r : ℝ), closedBall x r ⊆ U → V.weight (closedBall x r) = ENNReal.ofReal (∫ z in V.carrier ∩ closedBall x r, V.mult z ∂(μHE[n] : Measure (Amb n ℓ)))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 3 of the parent proof. There μ(B) = ∫⁻_{M ∩ B} ofReal θ dHⁿ by withDensity_apply and Measure.restrict_restrict, and θ is Hⁿ-integrable on M ∩ B by integrableOn_mult because B is a compact subset of U. This child is the sharper equality form of that step: the comparator-accepted declaration rsod_weight_closedBall_eq_ofReal_integral, reused here with its identical frozen type. The parent applies it to B = B_s(ζ) ⊆ U only to conclude μ(B) = ofReal(·) < ∞. The argument below is the accepted one.

Setting: n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^{n+ℓ}, V : RectifiableVarifold n ℓ U with carrier M and multiplicity θ, Hⁿ := μHE[n]. By definition μ_V := V.weight = (Hⁿ⌞M).withDensity(z ↦ ofReal(θ z)). Let x ∈ ℝ^{n+ℓ}, r ∈ ℝ, and B := B_r(x) (closed ball) ⊆ U.

1. B is closed and bounded in the finite-dimensional space ℝ^{n+ℓ}, hence compact (isCompact_closedBall), and B ⊆ U. By the structure field integrableOn_mult, θ is Hⁿ-integrable on M ∩ B.

2. B is Borel. By the definition of withDensity (withDensity_apply), μ_V(B) = ∫⁻_B ofReal(θ) d(Hⁿ⌞M). By Measure.restrict_restrict (B measurable), (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞B = Hⁿ⌞(B ∩ M). Since B ∩ M = M ∩ B, μ_V(B) = ∫⁻_{M ∩ B} ofReal(θ) dHⁿ.

3. θ ≥ 0 almost everywhere for Hⁿ⌞(M ∩ B).
 - M is Hⁿ-null-measurable (field nullMeasurableSet_carrier) and B is Borel, so M ∩ B is Hⁿ-null-measurable.
 - Hence Hⁿ⌞(M ∩ B)-almost every point lies in M ∩ B (ae_restrict_mem₀).
 - At such a point z ∈ M we have θ(z) > 0 (field mult_pos).

4. For a function that is integrable and almost everywhere nonnegative for a measure, ofReal of its integral equals the lower integral of ofReal of it (ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal). Apply this to θ and Hⁿ⌞(M ∩ B) using steps 1 and 3: ofReal(∫_{M ∩ B} θ dHⁿ) = ∫⁻_{M ∩ B} ofReal(θ) dHⁿ. With step 2: μ_V(B_r(x)) = ofReal(∫_{M ∩ B_r(x)} θ dHⁿ). ∎
proof_key_steps: closed ball compact and ⊆ U ⇒ θ integrable on M ∩ B_r(x) (integrableOn_mult)
withDensity_apply + Measure.restrict_restrict ⇒ μ_V(B) = ∫⁻_{M∩B} ofReal θ dHⁿ
θ ≥ 0 a.e. on M ∩ B (null-measurable carrier, ae_restrict_mem₀, mult_pos)
ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal

subproblems.title: Graph coordinates and the projection onto the rotated plane
subproblems.statement: For all n, l and every linear isometry q of R^(n+l): (i) graphPoint a b - graphPoint a' b' = graphPoint (a - a') (b - b') for a, a' in R^n, b, b' in R^l; (ii) |graphPoint a b|^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2; (iii) every z in R^(n+l) equals graphPoint a b for some a in R^n, b in R^l; (iv) the orthogonal projection P onto T_0 = rotatedPlane q = q(R^n x {0}) satisfies P(q(graphPoint a b)) = q(graphPoint a 0).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (q : Amb n ℓ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Amb n ℓ), (∀ (a a' : Rn n) (b b' : Rn ℓ), graphPoint a b - graphPoint a' b' = graphPoint (a - a') (b - b')) ∧ (∀ (a : Rn n) (b : Rn ℓ), ‖graphPoint a b‖ ^ 2 = ‖a‖ ^ 2 + ‖b‖ ^ 2) ∧ (∀ z : Amb n ℓ, ∃ (a : Rn n) (b : Rn ℓ), z = graphPoint a b) ∧ (∀ (a : Rn n) (b : Rn ℓ), (rotatedPlane q).starProjection (q (graphPoint a b)) = q (graphPoint a 0))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 1(a) of the parent proof: graphPoint is linear, graphPoint x y - graphPoint x' y' = graphPoint (x - x') (y - y'), and ||graphPoint x y||^2 = ||x||^2 + ||y||^2, via Fin.append and Fin.sum_univ_add. This is available as the comparator-accepted declaration lip_approx_graph_coordinates, reused here with its identical frozen type. The sibling graph_sqrt_two uses parts (i) and (ii). Parts (iii) and (iv) belong to the same frozen type and are proved exactly as in the accepted proof.

Notation. For a in R^n and b in R^l, graphPoint a b is the vector of R^(n+l) whose coordinate with index castAdd l i (i < n) is a_i and whose coordinate with index natAdd n j (j < l) is b_j (definition via Fin.append). Every index k in Fin (n+l) is of exactly one of these two forms (Fin.addCases). e_k is the k-th standard basis vector. H := horizontalPlane n l = span{e_(castAdd l i) : i < n}, T_0 := rotatedPlane q = q(H) (Submodule.map), and P is the orthogonal projection onto T_0 (starProjection).

1. (i) Both sides are vectors of R^(n+l); compare coordinates. Subtraction in EuclideanSpace is coordinatewise. At an index castAdd l i both sides equal a_i - a'_i, and at an index natAdd n j both sides equal b_j - b'_j (Fin.append_left, Fin.append_right). Hence graphPoint a b - graphPoint a' b' = graphPoint (a - a') (b - b').
2. (ii) For z in EuclideanSpace, |z|^2 = sum_k z_k^2. Split the sum over Fin (n+l) into the castAdd part and the natAdd part (Fin.sum_univ_add). For z = graphPoint a b this gives sum_i a_i^2 + sum_j b_j^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2.
3. (iii) Given z, put a := (z_(castAdd l i))_(i<n) in R^n and b := (z_(natAdd n j))_(j<l) in R^l. By the coordinate description of step 1, graphPoint a b and z have the same coordinates at every index, so z = graphPoint a b.
4. (iv) First, graphPoint a 0 = sum_i a_i e_(castAdd l i) (compare coordinates), so graphPoint a 0 lies in H and u := q(graphPoint a 0) lies in T_0 = q(H).
5. All castAdd-coordinates of graphPoint 0 b vanish, so <graphPoint 0 b, e_(castAdd l i)> = 0 for every i, hence (by linearity in the second argument) <graphPoint 0 b, h> = 0 for every h in H.
6. A linear isometry preserves inner products (polarization identity), so for every v = q(h) in T_0 we get <q(graphPoint 0 b), v> = <graphPoint 0 b, h> = 0. Thus w := q(graphPoint 0 b) lies in the orthogonal complement of T_0.
7. By step 1, graphPoint a b - graphPoint 0 b = graphPoint (a - 0) (b - b) = graphPoint a 0, so graphPoint a b = graphPoint a 0 + graphPoint 0 b and, q being linear, q(graphPoint a b) = u + w.
8. T_0 is finite dimensional, hence closed, and its orthogonal projection satisfies P u = u for u in T_0 and P w = 0 for w orthogonal to T_0. Therefore P(q(graphPoint a b)) = u = q(graphPoint a 0). This proves (iv). ∎
proof_key_steps: Coordinatewise description of graphPoint via Fin.append and Fin.addCases
(i) subtraction is coordinatewise
(ii) split the Euclidean norm sum over Fin (n+l) with Fin.sum_univ_add
(iii) read off a and b from the castAdd and natAdd coordinates
(iv) graphPoint a 0 lies in the horizontal plane and graphPoint 0 b is orthogonal to it
q preserves inner products, so q(graphPoint a 0) is in T_0 and q(graphPoint 0 b) is orthogonal to T_0
q(graphPoint a b) = q(graphPoint a 0) + q(graphPoint 0 b), and projecting onto T_0 keeps only the first summand

subproblems.title: Tilt-excess as a lower integral on a ball of finite weight
subproblems.statement: Let n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^{n+ℓ}, and V a rectifiable n-varifold in U in the sense of the contract (RectifiableVarifold n ℓ U). Write μ := V.weight and p_y := V.tangentProj y, and assume y ↦ p_y is μ-a.e. strongly measurable. Let ζ ∈ ℝ^{n+ℓ}, s > 0 and T a linear subspace of ℝ^{n+ℓ} with orthogonal projection P := T.starProjection, and assume μ(B_s(ζ)) < ∞ (B_s(ζ) the closed ball). Then ∫⁻_{B_s(ζ)} ofReal(hsNormSq(p_y − P)) dμ(y) = ofReal(s^n · V.tiltExcess ζ s T). Here hsNormSq(A) = Σ_{i<n+ℓ} ‖A e_i‖² and V.tiltExcess ζ s T = (s^n)^{-1} ∫_{B_s(ζ)} hsNormSq(p_y − P) dμ(y) (Bochner integral).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (U : Set (Amb n ℓ)) (V : RectifiableVarifold n ℓ U), AEStronglyMeasurable V.tangentProj V.weight → ∀ (ζ : Amb n ℓ) (s : ℝ) (T : Submodule ℝ (Amb n ℓ)), 0 < s → V.weight (closedBall ζ s) < ⊤ → ∫⁻ y in closedBall ζ s, ENNReal.ofReal (hsNormSq (V.tangentProj y - T.starProjection)) ∂V.weight = ENNReal.ofReal (s ^ n * V.tiltExcess ζ s T)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1(d), 1(e), 4 and the first equality of step 5 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 5, proof of 5.2, (10)). The finiteness μ(B_s(ζ)) < ∞ from parent step 3 is taken as an explicit hypothesis, so the lemma does not involve U.

Setting and notation. n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, N := n + ℓ, U ⊆ ℝ^N, V : RectifiableVarifold n ℓ U, μ := V.weight, p_y := V.tangentProj y. Hypotheses:
(H1) y ↦ p_y is μ-a.e. strongly measurable;
(H2) s > 0;
(H3) μ(B) < ∞, where B := B_s(ζ) is the closed ball.
T is a linear subspace of ℝ^N and P := T.starProjection is the orthogonal projection onto T. For a continuous linear A : ℝ^N → ℝ^N, hsNormSq(A) := Σ_{i ∈ Fin N} ‖A e_i‖², where e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 is the i-th standard basis vector. ‖·‖ is the Euclidean norm on vectors and the operator norm on continuous linear maps. Put h(y) := hsNormSq(p_y − P).

1. ‖p_y‖ ≤ 1 for every y ∈ ℝ^N. By definition (RectifiableVarifold.tangentProj), p_y is W.starProjection for a subspace W (the chosen approximate tangent space) when one exists, and 0 otherwise. In the first case ‖W.starProjection‖ ≤ 1 (Submodule.starProjection_norm_le); in the second, ‖0‖ = 0 ≤ 1. Likewise ‖P‖ ≤ 1 by Submodule.starProjection_norm_le.

2. For every continuous linear A: 0 ≤ hsNormSq(A) ≤ N‖A‖².
 - Nonnegativity: hsNormSq(A) is a sum of squares.
 - Upper bound: ‖e_i‖ = 1, so ‖A e_i‖ ≤ ‖A‖ ‖e_i‖ = ‖A‖ (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm). Hence ‖A e_i‖² ≤ ‖A‖², since squaring is monotone on [0, ∞). Summing over the N indices gives hsNormSq(A) ≤ N‖A‖².

3. 0 ≤ h(y) ≤ 4N for every y. By the triangle inequality and step 1, ‖p_y − P‖ ≤ ‖p_y‖ + ‖P‖ ≤ 2. So by step 2, 0 ≤ h(y) ≤ N‖p_y − P‖² ≤ N · 2² = 4N. In particular |h(y)| ≤ 4N for every y.

4. The map c : A ↦ hsNormSq(A − P), from continuous linear maps of ℝ^N to ℝ, is continuous. Indeed c(A) = Σ_i ‖(A − P) e_i‖² is a finite sum. Each summand is the composite of continuous maps: A ↦ A − P, then evaluation at the fixed vector e_i (A ↦ A e_i is continuous linear in A), then the norm, then squaring.

5. h = c ∘ (y ↦ p_y) is μ-a.e. strongly measurable. It is the composite of the continuous map c (step 4) with the map y ↦ p_y, which is μ-a.e. strongly measurable by (H1) (Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable).

6. h is μ-integrable on B. We have μ(B) ≠ ∞ by (H3), h is μ-a.e. strongly measurable (step 5), and |h| ≤ 4N everywhere (step 3). So Measure.integrableOn_of_bounded applies: a bounded a.e. strongly measurable function on a set of finite measure is integrable there.

7. h is integrable on B (step 6) and h ≥ 0 everywhere (step 3). So ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal, applied to μ restricted to B, gives ofReal(∫_B h dμ) = ∫⁻_B ofReal(h) dμ.

8. By definition (RectifiableVarifold.tiltExcess), V.tiltExcess ζ s T = (s^n)^{-1} ∫_B h dμ. By (H2), s^n > 0, in particular s^n ≠ 0. Hence s^n · V.tiltExcess ζ s T = s^n · ((s^n)^{-1} ∫_B h dμ) = ∫_B h dμ (mul_inv_cancel_left₀).

9. By steps 7 and 8: ∫⁻_{B_s(ζ)} ofReal(hsNormSq(p_y − P)) dμ(y) = ofReal(∫_B h dμ) = ofReal(s^n · V.tiltExcess ζ s T). ∎
proof_key_steps: ‖p_y‖ ≤ 1 (p_y is an orthogonal projection, Submodule.starProjection_norm_le, or 0) and ‖P‖ ≤ 1
hsNormSq A ≤ (n+ℓ)‖A‖² from ‖A e_i‖ ≤ ‖A‖, hence 0 ≤ hsNormSq(p_y − P) ≤ 4(n+ℓ)
A ↦ hsNormSq(A − P) is continuous, so y ↦ hsNormSq(p_y − P) is μ-a.e. strongly measurable
bounded + a.e. strongly measurable + μ(B_s(ζ)) < ∞ ⇒ integrable on B_s(ζ) (Measure.integrableOn_of_bounded)
ofReal_integral_eq_lintegral_ofReal: ofReal ∫_B h dμ = ∫⁻_B ofReal h dμ
s^n · tiltExcess ζ s T = ∫_B h dμ since s^n ≠ 0 (mul_inv_cancel_left₀)

subproblems.title: The graph map of a 1-Lipschitz function is sqrt(2)-Lipschitz
subproblems.statement: Let n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, q a linear isometry of ℝ^{n+ℓ}, f : ℝ^n → ℝ^ℓ and D ⊆ ℝ^n, and assume f is 1-Lipschitz on D. Write F(x) := q(graphPoint x (f x)). Then (a) ‖F(x) − F(x')‖ ≤ √2 ‖x − x'‖ for all x, x' ∈ D; and (b) if f(0) = 0 and 0 ∈ D, then ‖F(x)‖ ≤ √2 ‖x‖ for every x ∈ D.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (q : Amb n ℓ ≃ₗᵢ[ℝ] Amb n ℓ) (f : Rn n → Rn ℓ) (D : Set (Rn n)), LipschitzOnWith 1 f D → (∀ x ∈ D, ∀ x' ∈ D, ‖q (graphPoint x (f x)) - q (graphPoint x' (f x'))‖ ≤ Real.sqrt 2 * ‖x - x'‖) ∧ (f 0 = 0 → (0 : Rn n) ∈ D → ∀ x ∈ D, ‖q (graphPoint x (f x))‖ ≤ Real.sqrt 2 * ‖x‖)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 1(a)-1(c) of the parent proof, stated for an arbitrary set D on which f is 1-Lipschitz; the parent applies it with D = B^n_R(0). The graph-coordinate identities of step 1(a) come from the sibling child graph_coordinates, i.e. the accepted declaration lip_approx_graph_coordinates n ℓ q. Only parts (i) and (ii) are used:
(i) graphPoint a b − graphPoint a' b' = graphPoint (a − a') (b − b');
(ii) ‖graphPoint a b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖².
Parts (iii)-(iv) are not used.

Setting. n, ℓ ∈ ℕ, q a linear isometry (LinearIsometryEquiv) of ℝ^{n+ℓ}, f : ℝ^n → ℝ^ℓ, and D ⊆ ℝ^n with f 1-Lipschitz on D (LipschitzOnWith 1 f D). Put F(x) := q(graphPoint x (f x)).

1. For x, x' ∈ D: ‖f x − f x'‖ = dist(f x, f x') ≤ 1 · dist(x, x') = ‖x − x'‖ (LipschitzOnWith.dist_le_mul, dist_eq_norm).

2. For x, x' ∈ D: since q is linear, F(x) − F(x') = q(graphPoint x (f x) − graphPoint x' (f x')) (map_sub). Since q preserves norms (LinearIsometryEquiv.norm_map), and by (i), ‖F(x) − F(x')‖ = ‖graphPoint x (f x) − graphPoint x' (f x')‖ = ‖graphPoint (x − x') (f x − f x')‖.

3. By (ii) and step 1: ‖graphPoint (x − x') (f x − f x')‖² = ‖x − x'‖² + ‖f x − f x'‖² ≤ 2‖x − x'‖² = (√2 · ‖x − x'‖)². This uses (√2)² = 2 (Real.sq_sqrt, as 0 ≤ 2) and ‖f x − f x'‖² ≤ ‖x − x'‖², which is step 1 squared (both sides nonnegative).

4. Both a := ‖graphPoint (x − x') (f x − f x')‖ and b := √2 · ‖x − x'‖ are ≥ 0, and for nonnegative reals a² ≤ b² implies a ≤ b (pow_le_pow_iff_left₀ with exponent 2 ≠ 0). With step 2 this gives ‖F(x) − F(x')‖ ≤ √2 ‖x − x'‖ for all x, x' ∈ D, which is part (a).

5. graphPoint 0 0 = 0. By (i) with a = a' = 0 and b = b' = 0: 0 = graphPoint 0 0 − graphPoint 0 0 = graphPoint (0 − 0) (0 − 0) = graphPoint 0 0. Hence if f(0) = 0, then F(0) = q(graphPoint 0 (f 0)) = q(graphPoint 0 0) = q(0) = 0 (map_zero).

6. Part (b): assume f(0) = 0 and 0 ∈ D, and let x ∈ D. Apply part (a) to x and x' = 0 ∈ D, and use F(0) = 0 from step 5: ‖F(x)‖ = ‖F(x) − F(0)‖ ≤ √2 ‖x − 0‖ = √2 ‖x‖. ∎
